title: Druxt Auth 0.5.0; two ways to sign in without leaving your site
description: Simple OAuth 6 removed the password grant. Druxt Auth 0.5.0 gets it working again through a contrib module, and the authorization code grant now takes credentials too, so a Nuxt front end signs people in without sending them to Drupal.

content.html: Every Druxt site I have built signs people in by sending them somewhere else to do it: out to Drupal's login page, on to a consent screen, and eventually back. With 0.5.0 the username and password go into a form on your own site instead, either through the authorization code grant or through the password grant. They are not interchangeable.
If you have not used it, Druxt Auth wires Nuxt's auth module to Simple OAuth on the Drupal side. It is Nuxt 2 for now, because the auth layer underneath it is.

content.alt: The druxtjs.org getting-started tutorial with a Sign in to edit dialog open over it, asking for a username and password
content.caption: Signing in happens on the page you were reading. The dialog says it plainly: reading the docs never needs an account.

content.html: The first is the authorization code grant, now able to take credentials directly. Druxt Auth signs the visitor in through Drupal's JSON login route first, so the authorize step finds a session waiting and returns a code without rendering anything:

content.title: Authorization code, handed credentials
content.highlighted: // Nuxt 2 await $auth.loginWith('drupal-authorization_code', { credentials: { name, pass }, })

content.html:
• No client secret in the app: underneath it is still authorization code with PKCE.
  • You get a real Drupal session, which matters if your editors use Drupal's own screens through the frontend, and logout() ends it.
  • Drupal and the frontend have to look like one site to the browser, so it needs the proxy.

The second is the password grant. It shipped in 0.4.0, then Simple OAuth 6 took the grant out of Drupal and took this with it. 0.5.0 gets it working again, against Simple OAuth Password Grant, the contrib module that puts it back:

content.title: Password grant, through the server route
content.highlighted: // Nuxt 2 await $auth.loginWith('drupal-password', { data: { username, password }, })

content.html:
• No redirect, and no proxy needed: the credentials go to Drupal's token endpoint through Druxt Auth's own server route.
  • That route needs a server, so a statically generated site is out.
  • Tokens and nothing else. Drupal's own pages stay anonymous however signed in the frontend looks, until you set passwordSession, which does need the proxy.
Neither needs a form from you. 0.5.0 ships the sign-in too, a DruxtAuthLogin component and a Nuxt page at /user/login. Drop your own component of that name into components/ and it takes over.

Both of these post credentials to an endpoint, not to Drupal's login form, and a fair amount of Drupal's login behaviour lives on that form. Drupal's two-factor module interposes there. So does a forced password change, a terms-of-service gate, and anything else that alters it. Skip the form and you skip those with it, for the visitor you meant to help and for anyone else holding the password.

Rate limiting survives, in two places rather than one. The credential sign-in goes through core's auth controller, so core's flood control runs. The password grant never reaches that controller, so the contrib module runs its own flood control, registering under oauth2_password_grant.failed_login_ip rather than user.failed_login_ip. If someone is locked out that way, clearing the core flood entries will not release them.

None of that makes the credential options wrong. It makes them a trade, because the trip to Drupal is what ran whatever the login form enforced. If you need two factor, the redirect is still there, and calling loginWith without credentials asks for it. I already run two factor on a decoupled front end, through that same redirect. The flow is rougher than it will be.

paragraphs.title: What the login form was doing for you

content.html: Start with origin. The session cookie from that JSON login has to reach the authorize request, so druxt: { proxy: { api: true } } is what makes the first option work at all. Without it the form falls back to the redirect. Across separate domains the cookie would be third party, and the redirect is your only way in.

Consumers are next. A Consumer cannot be public and confidential at once, so a site running both flows needs two, with passwordClientId for the second. It also has to authorize automatically, or that step shows Drupal's consent page and the visitor sees Drupal anyway. On Simple OAuth 6 you need an OAuth2 scope as well, because it refuses every authorization request until one exists.

Last, a Drupal session already open in the browser is refused, rather than quietly signing the visitor in as whoever left it there. The error sets sessionInUse so your form can explain itself. To end it instead, point sessionLogout at a route you add on the Drupal side.

paragraphs.title: Three things that catch people out

content.html: druxtjs.org was rebuilt this month so Druxt renders its own docs, every docs page a node and the navigation a menu. It is the site I test sign-in against, with the password grant on a branch there rather than in production.

content.alt: A phone screen showing the sign-in dialog, credentials entered, then the tutorial page with an avatar in the header and an editor bar along the bottom
content.caption: The password grant on a phone, start to finish, with no navigation in between. The bar along the bottom is the editing work this is being built for.

content.html: The password grant was never Druxt Auth's to give. Simple OAuth 6 removed it because the OAuth security best practice says it must not be used, and only Drupal's OAuth server can mint a token.

Simple OAuth Password Grant puts it back, maintained by Christoph Niedermoser and Christian Foidl. Their README is blunt about it: use it with great care, for trusted first-party applications, and prefer the authorization code grant where you can. Thank you both.

So which one fits? If you can run a server and tokens are all you need, the password grant. If you need Drupal's own screens to know who is looking, or you want to keep the door open for two factor, the authorization code grant. If either is useful to you, 0.5.0 is out now:

content.title: Both halves
content.highlighted: composer require 'drupal/simple_oauth_password_grant' npm install druxt-auth@^0.5

content.html: What has kept you on the redirect?

paragraphs.title: Who put the password grant back

content.description: Druxt Auth, and the example app that runs both flows against a real Drupal. Sponsorship is what keeps Druxt maintained.
